title: How to become a graphic designer in Sri Lanka: an honest guide
excerpt: The skills employers here ask for, the portfolio that gets opened, where the work is, and how to research what the job pays instead of trusting a made-up figure.
body_html:
This is a practical route into graphic design work in Sri Lanka, written for someone starting from nothing or moving across from another job. It covers what the work is really like, the skills employers here actually ask for, how to build a portfolio that gets opened, where the work is, and how to find out what the job pays without relying on somebody's guess.

What the job actually is

A junior designer's week is less inventive than the course brochures suggest. You will resize an approved campaign into eleven formats, amend the artwork after the client changes a price, correct a supplied logo that arrived as a low-resolution PNG, and prepare a file the printer can process without ringing you. Original concept work exists, and it grows as you become more trusted, but the craft is production: accuracy, file discipline, and delivering on the day you said you would.

People who enjoy the job tend to be the ones who take satisfaction from a clean file and a job that comes back from press looking right. If the only appealing part is the creative brief, the first year will be a shock.

The skills that get asked for here

The three core applications. Photoshop for images, Illustrator for logos and vector artwork, InDesign for anything with pages. Studios in Colombo expect all three, not depth in one. Being fluent in Photoshop alone marks you as a social media producer rather than a designer, which is a fine job but a different one.

Print production knowledge. Bleed, trim, colour modes, spot colours, overprint, resolution for the size of the piece, and how to package a job so a press in Maradana can output it without a phone call. This is where self-taught designers most often come unstuck, and it is entirely learnable.

Typography. Not font collecting. Hierarchy, measure, leading, alignment, and the discipline to use two typefaces properly rather than six badly.

Sinhala and Tamil typesetting. This one is specific to working here and it is worth learning early. Much local material is trilingual, legacy non-Unicode fonts are still circulating in supplied copy, and a layout that looks correct on your machine can break on the client's. Learn the difference between Unicode and legacy Sinhala text, know which fonts render properly in InDesign with the correct composer settings, and get into the habit of asking for copy in Unicode. Designers who handle Sinhala and Tamil layout confidently are noticeably more employable in the local market than those who only work in English.

Digital tools alongside the Adobe set. Figma for interface and web work, and enough understanding of how a web page is built to hand over assets a developer can use. A great deal of the design work advertised locally is digital rather than print.

Generative AI, honestly used. Employers are asking about it. What they want is somebody who can speed up the dull parts and knows what must not be generated, not somebody who submits AI output as finished design.

Do you need a degree?

No, and this is genuinely a portfolio-first field. A degree or diploma from a recognised institution helps with HR screening, structured feedback and contacts, and it matters more for in-house roles at large organisations than at agencies. Nobody in a studio has ever hired on a transcript when the folio was weak.

Short focused training has a specific use: it fills the gaps you cannot see from tutorials, particularly production and typography, and it gives you deadlines. An Adobe Certified Professional pass, taken through Certiport, is useful evidence for a hiring manager who does not know you, especially at the point where your portfolio is still thin. It is not a substitute for work.

Building a portfolio that gets opened

Six to eight pieces, no fillers. Reviewers stop at the weakest piece, so cut anything you are defending.

  • Include one job that went to print. Even a menu for a family friend's café outranks a beautiful unbuilt concept, because it proves you can finish.
  • Show the constraint, not just the outcome. One paragraph per piece: the brief, the limitation, what you decided and why. Reviewers hire the thinking.
  • Include one piece with Sinhala or Tamil type set properly. Very few junior folios have this, and it is remembered.
  • Include one system, not just one artefact. A logo with its usage rules, or a set of five social templates that hold together, shows you can think past a single canvas.
  • Redesign something real, and say it is a redesign. A local product's packaging or a government form. Show the original, explain what fails, then show your version.
  • Present it as a PDF and a simple web page. Behance or a one-page site is fine. Make the PDF small enough to email.

Avoid unpaid spec work and design contests. They consume the time you need for your own portfolio and produce nothing you control.

Where the work is

Advertising and creative agencies, mostly in and around Colombo, take juniors and train them hard. In-house marketing teams at banks, insurers, telcos, retail chains, hotels and hospitals hire designers directly and often pay more predictably than small agencies. The apparel and export sector needs packaging, labelling, catalogues and buyer presentations, and it is a large and frequently overlooked employer of designers here. Printing companies employ pre-press and artwork staff, which is unglamorous and an excellent first job for learning production properly. Digital agencies and software companies need UI, social and product design. And there is remote and freelance work for overseas clients, which pays in foreign currency and is worth setting up carefully with your bank and an accountant rather than improvising.

Your first paid work will usually come from people who already know you: a small business, a school or university society, an NGO, a temple or church event, a friend starting a venture. Do those jobs properly, with a written scope and a deadline, and they become both portfolio pieces and referrals.

How to find out what it pays

Ignore any article, this one included, that quotes a salary figure for Sri Lankan designers. The market moves, the range across agency and in-house is wide, and most published numbers are recycled from nowhere. Research it directly instead.

  • Read current job advertisements on the local job boards and on LinkedIn. Many list a range or a band, and reading fifty adverts gives you a real picture of the going rate and the titles attached to it.
  • Ask two or three people doing the job now. Framed as "what band should I be asking for at my level", this is a normal conversation, not a rude one.
  • Ask recruiters what they are placing juniors at. It is their job to know.
  • For freelance rates, work from your own numbers: your target annual income, your realistic billable hours, your software subscriptions and equipment, then divide. Pricing by feel is how freelancers end up working for less than a salaried junior.
  • Remember that Adobe Creative Cloud is priced in foreign currency. Budget for the subscription in your rate rather than discovering it later.

A realistic twelve months

Months one to three: learn Photoshop, Illustrator and InDesign to a working standard and produce something finished in each. Months four to six: take on two or three small real jobs, one of which must go to print, and start the portfolio. Months seven to nine: add Figma or production depth depending on the direction you want, sit an Adobe Certified Professional exam if you want the external evidence, and rebuild your portfolio around your best six pieces. Months ten to twelve: apply, ask for feedback from every rejection, and take an internship or junior role even if the title is unexciting. The first job teaches you things no course can, because it comes with consequences.
